lesson.title: Identity and inverses

steps.headline: The identity matrix changes nothing. The inverse of A undoes A.

lead.text: The identity matrix I has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. I v = v for every v. The inverse A⁻¹ undoes A, so A⁻¹ A = I and A A⁻¹ = I.
The 2 × 2 identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It leaves every vector as it was.

reveal.text: You reasoned that undoing a map that does nothing needs no change. The identity is its own inverse.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc, from the entries a = 3, b = 1, c = 5 and d = 2.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by ad − bc.
If ad − bc were zero, this division would fail and there would be no inverse.

steps.headline: Find entry (2, 2) of the inverse of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by that number. What is entry (2, 2) of the inverse?

lead.text: The matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has ad − bc equal to 1, so dividing by it changes nothing.

reveal.text: You swapped the diagonal and negated the off-diagonal entry. The inverse of a shear is the shear in the opposite direction.

lead.text: A machine with matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ turned a hidden input v into the output (1, −2). Undo the machine to recover v.

lesson.orientation: Undo an invertible square map and recognise when an inverse cannot exist.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3. This time it gave back 17.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a matrix map with its inverse, and spot a matrix that has no inverse.

recap.keyIdea: An inverse undoes a map: A⁻¹A is the identity. A 2 × 2 matrix has one when ad − bc is not zero, and then A v = b is solved by v = A⁻¹b.

blocks.text: You found that the identity is its own inverse, inverted [(2, 1); (1, 1)] to get 2 in the corner, and recovered an input by undoing the map.

recap.nextHook: Undoing a map is the same as solving equations. Next: row reduction, which solves them without a formula.

hints: The machine did two things. Undo them in the opposite order.
Undo the adding first.
Take away the added amount, then undo the doubling.

misconceptions.feedback: That only undoes the adding. The doubling has to be undone as well.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You undid the last step first, then the one before it. An inverse map does just that.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A⁻¹ A = I: undoing A leaves every vector unchanged.

hints: The inverse undoes A. What is left when nothing happens?

misconceptions.feedback: A⁻¹ undoes A, so nothing of A is left. The result leaves every vector unchanged.
The zero matrix would send every vector to zero. Undoing a map leaves vectors as they were.

questions.onCorrect: Undoing A leaves every vector unchanged, which is what the identity matrix does.

questions.prompt: What is entry (1, 1) of the inverse of the 2 × 2 identity matrix?
hints: What does the identity matrix do to a vector?
Undoing a map that does nothing requires no change.
The inverse is the identity again. Read off its diagonal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The identity is its own inverse, so the entry is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is an off-diagonal entry. The identity's diagonal entries are the ones.

questions.onCorrect: The identity does nothing, so undoing it does nothing: it is its own inverse.

acceptedIdeas: The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inverse is built by dividing by ad − bc, which fails when it is zero.

questions.prompt: Why is there no inverse when ad − bc = 0?

choices.label: The formula divides by ad − bc, and you cannot divide by zero.
A matrix with a zero entry never has an inverse.
The zero matrix cannot be multiplied.

hints: Look at the last step of the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: Many matrices with zero entries have inverses. The test is the number ad − bc.
Any matrices of matching shape can be multiplied. The issue is the division in the formula.

questions.onCorrect: The formula divides by ad − bc, so a zero there means no inverse.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the others, then divide by that number.
Which diagonal entry of A lands in the position the question names?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The inverse is [(1, −1); (−1, 2)]. Multiplying it by A gives I.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a different diagonal entry. The two diagonal entries swap places.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the diagonal entries and divide by ad − bc, which is 1 here.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
The off-diagonal entries change sign.
Negate the entry in the top right of A.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.onCorrect: Negate the off-diagonal entry: the inverse shear goes the other way.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and the output was (1, −2). What is the first coordinate of v?
hints: Write out what A v equals, one row at a time.
The second row gives the second coordinate of v on its own.
Put that value into the first row and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second equation gives v₂ = −1. The first gives v₁ − 1 = 1, hence v₁ = 2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first coordinate of the output, not of the input.

questions.onCorrect: Undo the map: the second row gives v₂ = −1, and the first row then gives v₁ = 2.

hints: Find ad − bc.

misconceptions.feedback: Work out ad − bc. A zero there means no inverse.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 1 × 4 − 2 × 2 = 0, so there is no inverse.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (2, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: The matrix scales each axis separately.
Undo a multiplication by dividing by the same number.
Take the reciprocal of the matching diagonal entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Undo multiplication by −2 with multiplication by −1/2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the entry of A itself. The inverse entry is its reciprocal.
The sign is missing. Undoing a negative scale is still negative.

questions.onCorrect: Undo multiplying by −2 by multiplying by −1/2. Diagonal matrices invert entry by entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ad − bc = 4 − 3 = 1, so the inverse is [(2, −3); (−1, 2)] and the entry is −3.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is entry (1, 2) of A⁻¹?
hints: Find ad − bc first.
The off-diagonal entries change sign.
Negate the entry in the top right of A, then divide by ad − bc.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The off-diagonal entries are negated.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc is 1, and the off-diagonal entry is negated: −3.
